You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write an essay of up to 500 words on why most product roadmaps fail.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
Most product roadmaps fail because they are asked to do two incompatible jobs at once. They are supposed to be a strategic instrument, a way of saying what matters and what doesn't, and they are also supposed to be a promise, a schedule of things that will exist by certain dates. Strategy requires the freedom to change your mind when the world tells you something new. Promises require that you don't. Put both demands on a single document and it will quietly become a promise, because promises are what other people remember.

The first failure, then, is that roadmaps get treated as commitments by everyone except the people who wrote them. A sales leader sees a feature in the Q3 column and mentions it to a prospect. A support director tells an angry customer relief is coming in the spring. Marketing starts drafting the launch. By the time the product team learns something that should change the plan, the plan has been socialized into an obligation. Changing it now looks like failure rather than learning, so the team ships the thing anyway, late and diminished, and calls it a win.

The second failure is that roadmaps are usually lists of outputs rather than statements of intent. A row that says "notifications revamp" tells you nothing about what problem is being solved or how you would know if it worked. Teams building against output lists optimize for shipping, because shipping is the only thing being measured. You end up with a year of completed items and no discernible improvement in the business, which is how organizations arrive at the strange conclusion that they are executing well and losing anyway.

Third, roadmaps are built on estimates that everyone knows are fiction and no one is allowed to say so. Effort guesses made before discovery are wrong by large multiples, and they are wrong in one direction. So the calendar is fantasy from the first day, and every subsequent week is spent negotiating which parts of the fantasy to abandon. This is exhausting and corrosive, and it teaches engineers that planning is theater.

Fourth, most roadmaps are aggregations rather than choices. Each stakeholder gets something, so nothing gets enough. The document becomes a peace treaty among departments, which is a perfectly reasonable political achievement and a terrible allocation of attention. Real roadmaps say no loudly, and saying no loudly is expensive for the person holding the pen, which is why it so rarely happens.

What tends to work better is modesty about time and clarity about purpose. Be specific about what you are doing now, name the problem you expect to solve next and why it matters, and keep the far future deliberately vague, described in terms of the outcomes you are chasing rather than the features you imagine will produce them. Revisit it often enough that changing it feels normal. Tell the rest of the company how to read it, including which parts are firm and which are hypotheses.

None of this makes planning easy. It just stops the plan from lying.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Most product roadmaps fail because they pretend the future is more predictable than it is. They often present a neat sequence of features, dates, and milestones, creating the impression that product development is a matter of executing a known plan. In reality, products are built in uncertain environments. Customer needs change, competitors move, technical constraints emerge, and ideas that sound convincing in a meeting may fail when tested.

The first problem is that many roadmaps focus on outputs rather than outcomes. They promise features instead of describing the customer or business problem those features are meant to solve. This encourages teams to measure progress by how much they ship, not by whether the product becomes more useful. A feature can be delivered on time and still have no meaningful impact.

Roadmaps also become political documents. Sales teams want commitments they can share with prospects. Executives want evidence that strategic goals are being addressed. Customers want reassurance that their requests are coming. Product leaders often respond by adding more items and assigning dates before enough is known. The roadmap becomes a collection of promises to different stakeholders rather than a coherent expression of product strategy.

Another reason roadmaps fail is that they separate planning from learning. Teams may spend months building an item because it appears on the roadmap, even after research suggests that the underlying assumption is wrong. Changing direction can look like poor execution, so people continue with the plan to avoid difficult conversations. The roadmap, which should support decision-making, instead prevents it.

Overloaded roadmaps create a further problem. When everything is a priority, nothing is. Teams divide their attention across too many initiatives, dependencies multiply, and delivery slows. Dates begin to slip, confidence falls, and managers respond by demanding more detailed estimates. This adds administrative effort without reducing uncertainty.

A useful roadmap should not claim to know exactly what will be built far into the future. It should explain which problems matter, why they matter, what outcomes the organization seeks, and what assumptions need to be tested. Near-term work can be specific because the team has more evidence. Longer-term plans should remain flexible.

Most roadmaps do not fail because teams lack discipline. They fail because certainty is rewarded more than honesty. A roadmap succeeds when it helps people make better choices as new information arrives, not when it preserves an outdated plan.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_A: Signposting through ordinal markers ('The first failure', 'The second failure', 'Third', 'Fourth')
Rule-of-three list in paragraph 2 ('A sales leader sees...', 'A support director tells...', 'Marketing starts...')
tells_B: Heavy reliance on negative parallelism ('outputs rather than outcomes', 'features instead of describing', 'how much they ship, not by whether', 'promises... rather than a coherent expression', 'which should support decision-making, instead prevents it', 'not claim to know... It should explain', 'not fail because teams lack discipline. They fail because', 'when it helps people make better choices... not when it preserves')
Triads throughout ('features, dates, and milestones'; 'Sales teams want... Executives want... Customers want...'; 'dependencies multiply, and delivery slows')
Uniform, metronomic sentence rhythm across all paragraphs
Uplifting, neat recap ending with no friction or genuine emotion
Generic, abstract prose performing for a crowd with no concrete names, dates, or specific artifacts
